# Mixed metaphor and catachresis — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Mixed metaphor and catachresis. Run status: COMPLETED.

## How it works

- [statement] Quintilian (Institutio Oratoria 8.6.34-35) defines catachresis (abusio) as adapting the nearest available term for something with no proper term, and distinguishes it from metaphor, which is used when another term is available. (medium confidence) — https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:2007.01.0066:book%3D8:chapter%3D6 · keywords: Mixed metaphor and catachresis · also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catachresis
- [statement] Catachresis has several senses in current usage: categorical boundary crossing when no term exists (chair 'legs'), sound-alike substitution (ravished for famished), strained extension (Shakespeare's 'deepest winter in Lord Timon's purse'), and vaguer synonym substitution (job-seeker for unemployed). (low confidence) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catachresis

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] Kimmel (Journal of Pragmatics, 2010) analysed a corpus of British newspaper commentaries on the 2004/05 EU referenda (2,574 metaphors) and reports mixed metaphors at 39-62% of metaphors, with almost all ontologically mixed clusters comprehensible; he argues mixing is cognitively successful because it covers different aspects of a target domain. Figures are from search-result abstracts; the paper page returned HTTP 403. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378216609001222

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Merriam-Webster defines a mixed metaphor as a figure of speech combining inconsistent or incongruous metaphors, and lists it beside catachresis as strained use of words that may occur in error or for rhetorical effect. (low confidence) — https://www.merriam-webster.com/thesaurus/mixed%20metaphor
- [statement] A mix of metaphors is therefore not by itself evidence of error or machine authorship: classical rhetoric permits catachresis where no term exists, and corpus work finds human mixing is common and usually coherent. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378216609001222 · keywords: Mixed metaphor and catachresis · also: https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:2007.01.0066:book%3D8:chapter%3D6

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Quintilian (8.6.50) warns that many writers begin a figure with a tempest and end with a fire or a falling house, producing a hideously incongruous effect, and says never to mix metaphors. (low confidence) — https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:2007.01.0066:book%3D8:chapter%3D6
